## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)

- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)

- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-12: 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator — Technical Proposal

**Project Dyson, Phase 0A**
**Status:** Proposal for baseline. All numbers are engineering estimates at pre-Phase-A maturity. Confidence is low to medium; the basis for each figure is stated where it appears.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

The 0A Pathfinder is the one mission that turns Phase 0 from a paper study into a decision. It must give the KDP-0B board flight evidence, from the actual target, that the project-ending technologies work: excavation, beneficiation, primary Fe-Ni processing and containment. It must also show they work together, under autonomy, in microgravity, at a scale that can be extrapolated.

**Recommended architecture.** A single launch of about 25 t carries three elements:

1. **Carrier/Orbiter (C/O).** A 100 kWe solar-electric carrier, krypton baseline, with one iodine string flown for life data. It handles transfer, hover/orbit operations, ejecta monitoring, relay and product return.
2. **Surface Plant Module (SPM).** An anchored, roughly 8 t plant. It carries:
   - a 75 kWe sun-tracking array;
   - 150 kWh of storage;
   - a beneficiation train;
   - a centrifugal induction furnace at full 0B unit scale;
   - a subscale carbonyl refining cell;
   - integral containment.
3. **Two flight-standard mining robots** from the bom-0-2 design. They are powered over a 2 kV tether, carry 20 kWh batteries, and supply the plant with sealed regolith canisters.

A small **Product Shuttle** lifts cast Fe-Ni to the carrier. The carrier returns about 300 kg of product toward SEL1 and drops a 5–10 kg sample capsule at an Earth flyby.

**Design philosophy: "full-scale units, subscale plant; gravity-independent processes."** Every unit process with scale-sensitive physics flies at the size 0B will use. This covers the robot, the excavation head, the crucible and the canister port. Plant throughput is about 1/9–1/12 of the 0B reference.

Every unit process is designed to create its own body force, by centrifuge or forced feed. That way ground tests stay valid and the flight result extrapolates.

**Key numbers (current best estimate)**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Launch mass | 24.8 t (range 21–27 t, depending on target Δv) |
| Dry mass, all elements | ≈16 t incl. 20% margin |
| Surface power | 75 kWe BOL at 1 AU; ~55 kW peak demand |
| Feed processed (full success) | ≥40 t regolith |
| Product (full success) | ≥4 t Fe-Ni, as ~55 kg centrifugally cast rings |
| Containment verification floor | escaping mass fraction measurable to 1×10⁻⁴ |
| Surface campaign | 12 months primary; 24+ months extended (SPM stays) |
| Launch / arrival / KDP-0B evidence | 2032–33 / 2034–35 / 2035–36 |

**Cost (bom-0-12 line, 0A only):** **$1.3–3.0B, point estimate $2.0B**, including a 25% project-held reserve. Launch, ops, ground segment and propellant are excluded; those sit in bom-0-8, 0-9, 0-10 and 0-16. Including them, the full-mission view is **$1.7–3.8B**. The 0B share of this line is **$0**.

**Position on round-2 figures**
- I agree with Claude's range in structure but narrow it.
- Gemini's $1.8–2.5B is plausible as a centre but too narrow for a low-confidence, first-of-kind estimate.
- GPT's $0.6–1.5B hardware figure is too low for ~16 t dry of first-of-kind industrial flight hardware plus a 100 kW SEP stage. GPT's $0.3–0.9B delivery figure is too high for a single launch. Details are in §9.

## 2. Purpose, Scope and Boundaries

### 2.1 What the Pathfinder must prove (and nothing more)

The pathfinder exists to retire the risks that would end the project at KDP-0B. Per D-02, those must reach **TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers**. Flight at the candidate 0B target is the most relevant environment available. The demonstration is subscale in plant throughput, so I claim **TRL 6 for the 0B system** and **TRL 7 for the demonstrator configuration**.

| # | Project-ending question | Pathfinder answer |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Can we hold position and react excavation loads on a weak, possibly rubble-pile surface? | SPM anchoring plus robot self-anchoring; in-situ pull tests to 2 kN |
| Q2 | Can we excavate and move regolith to a plant at useful rates without losing it? | ≥0.8 t/day sealed-canister feed loop |
| Q3 | Does beneficiation (comminution + magnetic separation) work in µg on real material? | Centrifugal mill + magnetic drum; measured grade and recovery |
| Q4 | Can we melt, separate slag and cast Fe-Ni in µg, at full unit scale? | 50 kg-batch spinning induction crucible |
| Q5 | Can the product meet a Phase 1 specification, particularly sulfur? | In-situ assay + Earth lab assay of returned samples; carbonyl purity route |
| Q6 | Can we contain excavation fines, process dust and off-gas to a licensable level, and prove it? | Direct ejecta measurement from the carrier and perimeter sensors |
| Q7 | Can tethered robots, plant and power operate autonomously across up to ~20 min one-way light-time? | ≥72 h unattended production runs |
| Q8 | Does maintenance-by-robot work? | Robot replacement of plant ORUs (filters, mill liners, crucible) |

| bom-0-4 Cargo Tugs | No tug qualification here. The carrier shares PPU/thruster families where possible and flies one iodine string as a life-data source. |
| bom-0-5 Site Power | Pathfinder array/PMAD/storage is a subscale instance of the 0-5 design; builds carried here. |

### 2.3 What the Pathfinder is *not*

- **It is not a production asset.** About 4 t of product has no economic value. Scope creep toward "small 0B" is a named risk (R-14).
- **It is not a crewed-capable vehicle.** Docking and servicing interfaces and structural reserve are provided; no human-rating.
- **It is not a technology zoo.** Every payload must map to Q1–Q8 or to a D-05 open decision.

---

## 3. Design Philosophy (Opinionated)

1. **Full-scale units, subscale plant.** These fly at 0B unit size:
   - the robot;
   - the excavation head and its containment skirt;
   - the sealed canister and docking port;
   - the crucible (50 kg batch);
   - the magnetic separator drum width.

   Throughput is reduced by running fewer units at lower duty. This avoids the classic pathfinder trap: proving a process at a scale whose physics, such as melt surface-to-volume ratio, dust generation per cut, or seal wear, does not extrapolate.

2. **Make every process gravity-independent.** If the furnace works because it spins at about 1 g at the wall, it behaves almost identically on Earth and at the asteroid. Ground test then becomes predictive, and the flight test confirms rather than discovers. Where a process cannot generate its own body force, such as excavation or particle transport, use positive mechanical containment, never ballistic transfer.

3. **Sealed batch logistics over continuous open flow.** Robots fill sealed 50 L canisters and dock them to the plant. Regolith is never in free flight outside an enclosure. This is the single biggest containment lever.

4. **Measure containment directly.** A mass balance (in versus out) cannot verify 99.9% containment, because accounting error is about ±1%. The pathfinder must detect escaping material directly and quantify it one order of magnitude below the interim ceiling.

5. **Graceful partial success.** Minimum mission success comes from the excavation and containment chain alone, which are the hardest licence and physics risks. Processing failures must not kill excavation data, and vice versa.

6. **Fly what 0B will fly.** The same PMAD voltage (2 kV robot bus), the same autonomy architecture and the same canister standard. Anything pathfinder-unique must be justified.

7. **Leave infrastructure behind.** The SPM stays on the surface and keeps operating as a long-duration environment and degradation testbed. It has 0B power and data interconnects in case the 0B site is co-located.

---

**Why centrifugal casting.** In a spinning crucible, the denser metal (ρ ≈ 7.9 t/m³) migrates to the outer wall. Silicate slag (ρ ≈ 2.8–3.3 t/m³) forms an inner annulus. This replaces gravity settling, which is impossible in µg.

The resulting product is a ring of roughly r_in 0.20 m, r_out 0.25 m, height 0.10 m. That is about 7 L, or about 55 kg. A ring is a convenient handling unit for the shuttle and for the receiving node.

At r = 0.25 m, 60 rpm (ω ≈ 6.3 rad/s) gives about 1 g at the wall. A ground test at 120–170 rpm (2–4 g) bounds the 1 g terrestrial perturbation to ≤25–50%.

### 4.5 Why two primary-processing routes (decision at PDR)

Native Fe-Ni in ordinary chondrites is intergrown with troilite (FeS). The Fe–FeS eutectic is at 988 °C, so the melt route will dissolve sulfur into the metal unless the slag chemistry removes it. Above about 0.05–0.1 wt% S, Fe-Ni becomes hot-short and is a poor structural material.

The carbonyl (Mond-type) route leaves sulfur in the residue and yields very high-purity Fe/Ni. It also deposits directly onto mandrels, which may suit thin Phase 1 structures. The cost is a toxic, high-pressure CO loop, which is itself a containment test.

**Recommendation**
- Fly the melt route as baseline: robust and high throughput.
- Fly a carbonyl cell at about 1/10 of furnace throughput as a co-primary experiment.
- Confirm or delete the carbonyl cell at PDR, based on bom-0-11 sulfur-partitioning tests on real meteorite feed and on the Phase 1 purity specification from bom-0-13.

Deleting it saves about $40–80M and about 300 kg. I would not delete it unless ground tests show the melt route reaches S ≤ 0.05% with in-situ slag.

### 5.2 Δv and propellant (rocket equation, Kr Hall at Isp 1,800 s, vₑ = 17.7 km/s)

**Thrust and cruise times**
- Thrust at 75 kW to the PPUs, η = 0.60: T = 2ηP/vₑ ≈ 5.1 N.
- Outbound acceleration ≈ 2.1×10⁻⁴ m/s². That is ≈275 days of thrusting, giving 1.5–2 years of cruise with coasts and array power falloff.
- Return acceleration ≈ 6.4×10⁻⁴ m/s². That is ≈75 days of thrusting.

**Target selection requirement (to bom-0-1):** round-trip SEP Δv ≤ 9 km/s; preferred ≤ 8 km/s. Every 1 km/s of outbound Δv costs about 1.5 t of launch mass.

**Propellant choice (relation to D-05).** For the pathfinder I recommend krypton for the mission-critical strings, with one iodine string as an in-flight life test. D-05 governs the production supply line. The pathfinder needs only about 8.6 t, which costs roughly $3–10M at $300–1,000/kg Kr, and it cannot afford a low-TRL thruster on the critical path.

This is a deliberate exception, flagged for owner confirmation. It still feeds D-05 with about 3,000–6,000 h of high-power iodine operating data in deep space.

### 5.4 Thermal rejection

- **Waste heat:** ≈50 kW peak, since nearly all electrical input ends as heat.
- **Radiator sizing:** at 350 K and ε = 0.85, two-sided gross emission ≈1,450 W/m². After allowing for asteroid surface IR and solar backload, take ≈850–900 W/m² net. That gives **≈60 m² of panel** (planform), edge-on to the sun.
- **Furnace coil and crucible cooling:** a dedicated 450–500 K loop with its own panel section, to keep the low-temperature loop small.
- **Dust:** electrodynamic dust shield (EDS) electrodes on the radiator and array leading edges. The degradation rate (ε, α vs time) is measured continuously; this is a key 0B input.

### 5.5 Anchoring and stability

- **Gravity:** a 300 m body at 2,000 kg/m³ has GM ≈ 1.9 m³/s², surface g ≈ 8×10⁻⁵ m/s², and escape velocity ≈ 0.16 m/s. The SPM weighs about 0.7 N.
- **Loads:** robot reactions are taken by the robots' own anchors (bom-0-2 scope). SPM anchor loads come from mill and furnace spin-up torques (balanced by counter-rotating pairs), shuttle departure, and tether snatch. The design load is ≤500 N.
- **Anchors:** six legs, each with a helical screw anchor plus a backup penetrator (dual mechanisms for rubble-pile uncertainty). Each anchor is pull-tested in situ to 2 kN, giving ≥4× margin.
- **Fallback:** if anchoring fails, SPM operates "leaning" with low-thrust hold-down using cold gas (limited duration). In parallel, the robots run an excavation-and-containment-only campaign into canisters retrieved by the shuttle. This preserves minimum success (§7).
- **Target constraint:** rotation period ≥ 4 h. Faster spin can put the equatorial centrifugal term above gravity, making the regolith unretained.

### 5.7 Containment and verification

**Interim design ceiling, proposed per D-03 and pending bom-0-15 and the licensing state:**
- escaping mass ≤ **1×10⁻³ of mass handled** (≥99.9% containment), all particle sizes;
- no intentional release;
- off-gas: sulfur and CO losses ≤ 1×10⁻³ of inventory per cycle.

The pathfinder is **not** designed to meet the ceiling with margin and stop. It is designed to **measure the achieved loss fraction down to 1×10⁻⁴**, so the licensing state can set a final number from data. This follows ALARP.

**Verification chain**

| Measurement | Instrument | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| Ejecta plume, 10 µm–10 cm | C/O-mounted scanning lidar + high-res stereo cameras at 1–5 km | Mass flux to ~0.1 g/min within 500 m |
| Fine dust flux, >1 µm | Impact detectors on 4 perimeter masts (50–150 m) | Flux to 10⁻⁶ g/m²/h |
| Local deposition | Witness plates, robot-read with microscope camera | Monthly maps |
| Off-gas | Mass spectrometers inside and outside the enclosure | ppm-level leak rates |
| Skirt and port seal performance | Pressure-decay and optical gap sensors | Per cycle |

**Calibration:** controlled tracer releases of known mass and size distribution, with distinctively shaped glass beads, early in the campaign.

**Escape physics:** with v_esc ≈ 0.16 m/s, anything leaving at more than cm/s is effectively lost. This is why ballistic or pneumatic transfer is banned.

## 6. Autonomy, Control and Communications

### 6.1 Light-time and autonomy layering

One-way light-time ranges from 0.5 to 20 min, depending on target geometry. Round-trip control is impossible for anything faster than campaign planning.

```
 LAYER            LOOP TIME      WHERE           AUTHORITY
 L0 Reflex        1 ms–1 s       robot/plant     servo, seal, arc-fault trip, crucible breach dump
 L1 Task          1 s–10 min     robot/plant     dig cycle, canister dock, batch melt, ORU swap
 L2 Coordination  min–hours      SPM executive   robot traffic, power scheduling, day/night plan
 L3 Campaign      daily–weekly   GROUND          goals, envelopes, parameter sweeps, test matrix
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Fault protection: L0/L1 must reach a safe state in ≤5 s on containment breach,
 HV fault, or crucible anomaly; SPM survives ≥72 h in safe mode without ground.
```

**Requirements**
- **AUT-1:** ≥72 h unattended production with both robots, at least 3 times during the campaign. This is the key autonomy TRL 6 evidence.
- **AUT-2:** ground commands are goals and envelopes (e.g., "process 8 canisters at furnace profile B"). No real-time joystick operations.
- **AUT-3:** a hard-wired, ground-commandable kill path independent of flight software, for licensing.
- **AUT-4:** robots detect and avoid tether entanglement and crossing.
- **AUT-5:** onboard anomaly logging at full rate, with prioritised downlink.

### 6.2 Communications

| Link | Terminal | Rate (design) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| C/O ↔ Earth | 3 m Ka/X, ~100 W RF | 2–15 Mbps at 1–1.5 AU (34 m DSN, Ka) | Primary science and engineering downlink |
| SPM ↔ Earth | 1.5 m Ka/X | 0.5–4 Mbps at 1.5 AU | Direct-to-Earth; primary after C/O departs |

bom-0-9 must cost this as procured DSN time or a commercial 18–34 m equivalent. Indicatively that is ~1,500–3,000 h/yr during operations.

### 9.4 Disagreements with round-2 figures

**Claude ($1.5–4B).** Directionally right. My range is narrower on the high side because launch, ops and propellant are explicitly split out to their own lines. The $4B tail implicitly double-counts those or assumes agency-style $200k/kg throughout.

**Gemini ($1.8–2.5B).** The centre is plausible and close to my $2.0B point. However, a ±16% band on a first-of-kind, TRL-2–3 industrial payload is not credible. Historical cost growth on first-of-kind planetary missions is commonly 30–60%. The band should carry the low confidence everyone agreed it has.

**GPT ($0.6–1.5B hardware + $0.3–0.9B delivery).**
- *Hardware is too low.* $0.6B would buy about 16 t dry at roughly $40k/kg, which is below even commercial GEO-satellite pricing for hardware that includes a novel furnace, robots, an anchored lander and 100 kW SEP. A smaller pathfinder could hit $0.6–0.9B, but only by one or more of:
  - dropping to one robot;
  - deleting product return;
  - shrinking to ~30 kW;
  - flying non-full-scale crucibles.

  Each of these forfeits a TRL 6 claim. That is the wrong trade for a gate whose purpose is no-waiver evidence.
- *Delivery is too high* for a single launch, unless it embeds ops or a two-launch architecture. I recommend designing to one launch.

## 11. Manufacturing and Integration Considerations

- **Model philosophy.**
  - Carrier: protoflight, using commercial SEP elements.
  - SPM bus: protoflight.
  - Processing payload: full EM → QM → FM. This is first-of-kind and project-critical, and it is the part where test-as-you-fly matters most.
- **Dirty integration.** The processing payload and robots must be tested with simulant and real meteorite-analog material, then cleaned for flight. Design for decontamination: sealed enclosures with bake-out and blow-down ports. Avoid untestable "never-been-dirty" mechanisms.
- **Long-lead and unusual items:**
  - space-rated 30 kW, 10–50 kHz induction power supply (no flight heritage at this power);
  - SmCo magnet assemblies (NdFeB loses coercivity above ~80–150 °C);
  - refractory crucibles (zirconia/alumina/BN-lined; vendor qualification);
  - high-pressure CO components (industrial heritage, space-qualification needed);
  - 2 kV slip rings and tether reels.
- **Commonality.** The PMAD 2 kV bus, canister standard, docking port, and robot ORU interfaces are defined once in bom-0-2, 0-3 and 0-5, and flown identically. A pathfinder-only interface variant requires a waiver.
- **Handling the stack.** The SPM is stowed at ~4.6 m Ø × 9 m, with arrays and radiators folded. A large-fairing launch is needed; this is a design driver tied to R-03.

## 12. Open Engineering Questions

1. **Sulfur partitioning.** What S content does melt-route Fe-Ni reach using only in-situ slag? This decides the carbonyl cell, and possibly the 0B process route. Need real-chondrite ground tests by PDR.
2. **Phase 1 product spec.** What composition, form and tolerance does Phase 1 actually require? The pathfinder spec in §7 is a placeholder; it must be frozen by CDR.
3. **Final containment number.** The 10⁻³ interim ceiling needs a debris-environment model of the target's heliocentric neighbourhood and Earth-crossing fraction, plus licensing-state input. Is 10⁻⁴ measurement floor sufficient?
4. **Pathfinder target = 0B target?** I argue yes, for TRL relevance. If the 0B target is unknown at pathfinder CDR, how representative must a surrogate be?
5. **Rubble-pile anchoring.** Is a 2 kN pull-out achievable in low-cohesion regolith? Alternative: net or bag-anchor concepts. The bom-0-1 scouts must return in-situ geotechnical data, so penetrometers on scouts are a recommended requirement.
6. **Night strategy.** Is "batch by day, warm hold by night" the right 0B choice, versus larger storage or thermal storage in the melt? The pathfinder should fly a test matrix covering both.
7. **Iodine exception.** Does the owner accept krypton as the pathfinder's critical-path propellant, with iodine as a demo string, under D-05?
8. **Product return value.** Is bulk delivery to SEL1 worth ~1 t of launch mass and $20–40M if the receiving node (bom-0-13) is not operating by ~2037?
9. **Rotation-period limits.** What is the minimum rotation period at which surface operations remain safe, given centrifugal versus gravitational acceleration?
10. **Tether voltage selection.** Should the 0B system go to 3 kV to cut tether mass? The pathfinder test plan includes 3 kV runs, but the flight baseline is 2 kV for margin.
11. **Crucible life.** Is ≥300 batches per crucible achievable? If not, crucible spares dominate the bom-0-14 mass flow for 0B.
12. **LEO precursor funding.** Will bom-0-11 fund the centrifugal-furnace free-flyer? If not, R-04 likelihood should be raised to 4.

### 6.1 Excavation and anchoring

Baseline toolset:

1. **Counter-rotating shallow cutter/auger pair** for regolith and weak aggregate.
2. **Low-force scoop/grapple** for loose fragments and diagnostic sampling.

Counter-rotation reduces torque but does not eliminate reaction forces. The load path is:

> Tool → local frame → distributed anchors/contact pads → asteroid.

Initial force-limited operation should use approximately **1–20 N commanded tool reaction**, expanded toward **50–100 N** only after site-specific holding capacity is established.

Anchoring options should remain open through scout characterization:

- Microspines for competent rough surfaces.
- Penetrators or screws for suitable granular material.
- Distributed contact pads with modest preload.
- Mechanical wrapping or grappling where local geometry permits.

Do not assume conventional “landing legs” provide an adequate mining foundation.

### 6.2 Closed beneficiation

Recommended sequence:

1. Meter feed from the acquisition enclosure.
2. Separate oversize particles.
3. Apply controlled mechanical agitation.
4. Recover ferromagnetic particles using adjustable magnetic gradients.
5. Reprocess selected middlings.
6. Transfer concentrate to sealed process cartridges.

**No gravity-fed chute is a critical dependency.** Use positive-displacement screws, pockets, brushes or mechanically constrained transfer paths.

Electrostatic separation may be carried as a removable experiment, but should not be on the primary success path.

Baseline thermal process:

- Vacuum induction melting or another qualified electrically heated batch process.
- Approximately **1,600–1,850°C operating capability**, depending on alloy composition and process margin.
- Controlled solidification into simple moulds.
- Optional small hot-press/sintering experiment using the same characterized concentrate.

Preferred output forms:

- Small billets.
- Flat witness coupons.
- Tensile-test or bend-test specimens.
- Simple feedstock preforms for Phase 1 joining/manufacturing studies.

Do not attempt flight production of long wire, precision foil or finished swarm structures.

Containment is a primary mission objective, not housekeeping.

### 7.1 Architecture

Use nested barriers:

1. Surface-contact excavation hood with compliant perimeter features.
2. Internal baffles and ballistic particle traps.
3. Double-door transfer chambers.
4. Sealed beneficiation and furnace cartridges.
5. Dedicated retained-waste containers.

The surface hood is **not assumed hermetic**. An irregular, dusty asteroid surface makes that assumption unsafe.

The baseline uses mechanical collection rather than continuous gas flow, avoiding unnecessary consumables and a new source of particle acceleration.

Furnace vapours require cooler sacrificial collectors and filtered capture paths. Direct venting toward arrays, radiators, sensors or the surrounding environment is unacceptable.

### 7.2 Interim contamination requirement

Consistent with interim D-03, I recommend an initial engineering allocation of:

- **Uncontrolled solid release below 10⁻⁴ of handled mass over the campaign**, and
- No intentional release of tailings or test fragments.

For 300–1,000 kg handled, that corresponds to **30–100 g maximum uncontrolled solid release**.

This is **not a proposed universal legal threshold or an assertion of safety**. It is an initial design ceiling, subject to ALARP analysis, particle-population modelling, tests and licensing-state approval. Size distribution, velocity, chemistry and orbital persistence matter in addition to total mass.

A simple input/output scale balance cannot credibly verify such a small release fraction. Evidence must combine:

- Calibrated particle counters.
- High-speed local imaging.
- Witness collectors.
- Deposition monitors near sensitive surfaces.
- Ground-calibrated enclosure leakage models.
- Conservative upper bounds for unobserved particle sizes.

If measurement uncertainty exceeds the allocated release allowance, the mission cannot claim compliance merely because no plume was visible.

| Launch and transfer | 1–3 years | Successful rendezvous |
| Surface demonstration | 12–18 months | Relevant-environment evidence |
| Gate assessment | 6–12 months, partly overlapping | Independent technology and programme decision |

A credible planning interval is roughly **6–8 years from funded start to launch**, followed by transfer and surface operations. Scout results and launch opportunities can extend this.

### 11.1 Technology maturation claims

| Critical function | Likely entry readiness* | Required exit evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Asteroid enclosed excavation | TRL 3–4 | Integrated relevant-environment demonstration |
| Native-metal beneficiation in microgravity | TRL 3–4 | Repeatable separation with measured recovery |
| Vacuum Fe–Ni consolidation | TRL 3–5 | Characterized product from actual asteroid feed |
| Containment and release monitoring | TRL 3–4 | Validated release bounds and fault response |
| Autonomous anchored operation | TRL 4–5 | Sustained operations and recovery demonstrations |

\*Initial engineering judgments, to be replaced by a formal TRL/AD² assessment.

Under D-02, **KDP-0B requires every project-ending technology at TRL 6 in a relevant environment, without waivers**.

This pathfinder is necessary but not automatically sufficient. Industrial-scale continuous handling, megawatt power distribution, cargo operations or production furnace lifetime may require additional evidence under other BOM items. If their scaling risks remain project-ending, the gate remains closed.

### 11.2 Four discriminating gates

- **Target:** sufficient accessible native metal and demonstrated excavation.
- **Demand:** signed Phase 1 material/purity/quantity/date specification.
- **Economics:** updated full-cost comparison with Earth-supplied material and other credible sources.
- **Licence:** acceptable operational, contamination and end-state authorization.

A technically successful pathfinder does not compel 0B investment.

---

## 12. Cost estimate and treatment of round-2 figures

### 12.1 Direct bom-0-12 cost

| Element | 2026 USD |
|---|---:|
| Spacecraft bus, structure and proximity systems | $180–320M |
| EP hardware, excluding separately procured propellant | $70–140M |
| Dedicated power, storage and thermal systems | $100–190M |
| Excavation, manipulation and anchoring | $100–200M |
| Beneficiation, furnace and product handling | $140–280M |
| Flight containment hardware and instrumentation | $80–170M |
| Avionics, autonomy implementation and communications hardware | $50–90M |
| Integrated assembly, test and flight acceptance | $150–250M |
| Product metrology and calibration hardware | $40–80M |
| **Direct item subtotal** | **$910–1,720M** |

These include item-specific engineering. They exclude shared technology-development campaigns separately carried under bom-0-11.

### 12.2 Attributable costs booked to other items

| Allocation | 2026 USD |
|---|---:|
| Shared NRE, ground R&D and qualification | $180–400M |
| Launch and departure delivery | $200–450M |
| Communications/ground-network services | $30–70M |
| Mission operations | $80–160M |
| Propellant procurement and handling | $5–25M |
| Independent debris/licensing support | $15–40M |
| Dedicated spares/test replacements | $30–60M |
| Allocated organizational support | $20–50M |
| **External-line allocation subtotal** | **$560–1,255M** |

Combined pre-reserve estimate: approximately **$1.5–3.0B**.

Carry approximately **$0.35–0.85B** under the programme contingency/reserve line at this maturity, producing a rounded **$1.9–3.8B attributable mission envelope**. This is not a formal confidence interval; uncertainties are correlated.

### 12.3 Assessment of the round-2 proposals

- **Claude: $1.5–4B.** Broadly consistent with an all-in mission envelope. The low endpoint is optimistic for the proposed integrated scope; the upper endpoint is credible if qualification or target-access costs grow.
- **Gemini: $1.8–2.5B.** Plausible for a favourable target and mature propulsion, but too narrow as the current full uncertainty range.
- **GPT: $0.6–1.5B hardware plus $0.3–0.9B delivery.** The upper hardware estimate is plausible. I disagree with using the low hardware endpoint for a fully integrated, containment-qualified system with in-flight product testing. Delivery must also distinguish launcher price from total departure-stage and mission-injection services.

The dominant cost uncertainties are target-driven redesign, dusty mechanism qualification, containment verification and propulsion maturity—not the purchase price of raw metal or solar cells.

### 12.4 0A versus 0B

This item is entirely **0A**.

No industrial plant, cargo fleet, receiving node or continuing production workforce is included. Pathfinder data analysis can continue after the gate, but any extended industrial-support role requires an explicit new allocation. Do not assume an aging experiment can become a production asset.

---

## 13. Principal risks

| Risk | Consequence | Primary mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Metal present but not recoverable as native grains | No viable feedstock | Scout mineralogy and small-scale recovery evidence before design freeze |
| Surface cannot sustain tool loads | Acquisition fails | Distributed anchoring, low-force tools, multiple local sites |
| Dust jams transfers or degrades thermal surfaces | Early loss of capability | Closed transfers, sacrificial traps, redundant isolation |
| Furnace yields brittle or contaminated metal | Product unusable | Impurity screening, multiple process windows, onboard tests |
| Emissions cannot be measured adequately | Licence or gate failure | Calibrated particle instrumentation and conservative upper bounds |
| Industrial scale-up remains unproven | TRL 6 claim insufficient | Representative components and explicit scale-up qualification plan |
| EP life or propellant supply fails | Launch delay or unreachable target | Early life tests and retained alternate propulsion branch |
| Autonomous contact operations are unstable | Asset or target interaction hazard | Hardware safing, slow commissioning, validated force limits |
| Phase 1 demand changes | No industrial business case | Maintain demand gate; preserve Earth-supply fallback |
| Cost growth consumes broader 0A | Programme imbalance | Staged funding and independent descoping/termination reviews |

**Loss of the mission must not strand a 0B production commitment.** Long-lead industrial procurement should remain gated accordingly.

---

## 14. Open engineering questions

The highest-value unresolved questions are:

1. **Which asteroid actually offers accessible native Fe–Ni rather than merely a metal-rich remote signature?**
2. What feed-grade uncertainty is acceptable before committing to the flight furnace?
3. Which anchor/tool combination works across the measured surface-property distribution?
4. Can containment performance be bounded at the required level under real excavation conditions?
5. Which impurities control the Phase 1 material specification?
6. Can onboard testing support material acceptance, or is sample return indispensable?
7. Does induction melting remain preferable after accounting for concentrate morphology, crucible contamination and microgravity melt handling?
8. Which process features can legitimately reach TRL 6 at pathfinder scale, and which require larger demonstrations?
9. Can iodine propulsion meet life, compatibility and supply requirements on the mission schedule?
10. What end state minimizes long-term release risk without depending on indefinite active control?

## Bottom line

Fund a **single, substantial, instrumented asteroid process demonstrator**, not a symbolic scoop experiment and not a prematurely industrial factory.

The programme should purchase three defensible results:

1. **A measured resource-to-product process at the actual target.**
2. **A credible containment and environmental case.**
3. **Enough operational and material data to accept—or reject—0B without waivers or sunk-cost pressure.**

If native-metal processing fails, the mission can still succeed as a capability programme by establishing that result rigorously and directing Phase 1 toward Earth-supplied material rather than an unjustified industrial commitment.

# bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator: Consensus Synthesis

## Key Specifications

- **Mission count and crew.** All three models specify **1 uncrewed mission** to a single prospecting-qualified target NEA. No second asteroid visit and no reflight are baselined in this line. Claude holds a reflight long-lead option in bom-0-17, not here.
- **Scope.** All three test the full chain at the target: enclosed excavation → magnetic beneficiation → electrically heated batch melting/consolidation of **native Fe-Ni only** → product inspection → retained waste. All three exclude:
  - oxide or silicate reduction;
  - oxygen extraction;
  - cryogenic propellant production;
  - bulk production.
- **Propulsion type.** All three use **solar-electric Hall-thruster propulsion** for cruise, in the ~10–100 kWe class. The Δv envelope is target-dependent: Claude 5 km/s outbound; GPT 3–6 km/s useful. Claude and Gemini put cruise at **~1.5–2 years**; GPT gives 1–3 years.
- **Gate role (D-02).** All three state the pathfinder's purpose is to bring project-ending technologies to **TRL 6 in a relevant environment, without waivers**, at KDP-0B. Entry readiness is estimated at **TRL 2–5**, with TRL 4–5 delivered by ground R&D (bom-0-11) before design freeze.
- **Excavation and anchoring.** All three use **counter-rotating cutters** to cancel reaction torque, plus a **surface-sealed containment hood or skirt**. All three treat anchoring on weak or rubble-pile regolith as a top risk. Claude and Gemini carry a cold-gas or thrust hold-down fallback.
- **Containment.** All three treat containment as a primary mission objective with **no intentional release** of tailings, fines or test fragments. All three use sealed waste retention and an ALARP-based interim ceiling (D-03). Claude and GPT both state that a mass balance cannot verify the ceiling, so direct particle measurement is required: calibrated detectors, imaging and witness plates.
- **Thermal and power.** All three use **explicit pumped-loop radiators**. Claude and GPT add a separate warm loop at **~320–360 K** and a high-temperature loop at **~450–550 K**. All three schedule processing to available solar power rather than storing enough energy to run the furnace through the asteroid night.
- **Autonomy and comms.** All three use **layered onboard autonomy**: goal and envelope commanding, no real-time teleoperation, and hardware safing independent of flight software. Comms are **X/Ka-band HGA** over paid DSN or commercial ground service. Claude and GPT size returned data at **~1–10 GB/day** and reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day figure.
- **Cost split.** All three put this line **100% in 0A**. The **0B share is $0**: no industrial plant, fleet or production workforce is charged here.

## Divergent Views

- **Demonstrator scale.**
  - Claude recommends "full-scale units, subscale plant": a ~24.8 t launch stack, ~16 t dry, a 75 kWe surface plant, a full 0B-size 50 kg-batch crucible, ≥40 t feed and ≥4 t Fe-Ni.
  - Gemini prefers "end-to-end subscale": a 2.45 t wet single spacecraft with 15 kW, a 3 kW furnace, 5 kg/batch and ~0.5 kg Fe-Ni per batch.
  - GPT suggests a middle path: 6–8.5 t dry, 60–80 kWe, 300–1,000 kg feed and 10–80 kg product, with representative (not full-scale) contact surfaces and furnace conditions.
- **Cost of bom-0-12 and treatment of round-2 figures.**
  - Claude recommends **$1.3–3.0B (point $2.0B)** for the line, including 25% project reserve. Its full-mission view is $1.7–3.8B. Claude calls GPT's $0.6B hardware floor too low and GPT's $0.3–0.9B delivery too high for one launch.
  - Gemini prefers **$0.9–1.45B total**, including launch ($150–250M) and operations, and rejects $4B as front-loading capital. Gemini's text also rejects "Gemini's $2.5B", which is internally inconsistent.
  - GPT suggests **$0.91–1.72B direct** and **$1.9–3.8B fully burdened attributable** (point ~$2.7B), and rejects its own round-2 low endpoint.
- **Mission architecture and robots.**
  - Claude recommends three elements: a 100 kWe carrier/orbiter, an anchored Surface Plant Module, and **two flight-standard bom-0-2 robots** on 2 kV, 300 m tethers with 20 kWh batteries.
  - Gemini prefers a single integrated anchored spacecraft with an excavation head and no separate robots.
  - GPT suggests a single spacecraft with a 3–5 m arm and a short **1–2 kV** demonstrator tether branch, explicitly avoiding "importing an industrial robot fleet."
- **Propellant (D-05).**
  - Claude recommends **krypton for the critical-path strings** plus one iodine demo string. Claude flags this as a deliberate exception to D-05 needing owner confirmation.
  - Gemini prefers **iodine Hall thrusters (2 × 5 kW)** as baseline.
  - GPT suggests costing iodine with argon as the alternate per D-05, switching to a qualified alternative if iodine is immature.
- **Product return.**
  - Claude recommends a product shuttle, **~300 kg returned toward SEL1**, and a **5–10 kg Earth sample capsule**.
  - Gemini prefers on-board inspection of the coupon or ingot only.
  - GPT suggests **no sample return baselined**. GPT would decide before PDR whether Phase 1 acceptance requires Earth-lab data.
- **Containment ceiling and processing route.**
  - Claude recommends an interim ceiling of **≤1×10⁻³ of mass handled**, measured down to 10⁻⁴. Its process is centrifugal induction casting (~1 g at the wall, 1,550–1,600 °C) plus a subscale carbonyl cell for sulfur removal.
  - Gemini prefers a qualitative ALARP electrostatic Kapton/Kevlar shroud. Its process is induction melting with electromagnetic melt centering and inertia-driven casting.
  - GPT suggests a tighter **≤1×10⁻⁴ allocation (30–100 g over the campaign)**. Its process is vacuum induction at 1,600–1,850 °C with an optional hot-press/sintering experiment.

## Open Questions

1. **Scale validity of TRL 6.** Can a kg- to tonne-scale demonstration legitimately support a no-waiver TRL 6 claim for 0B units? Specific concerns are crucible life (≥300 batches?), dust-seal wear and melt surface-to-volume effects. Or do some project-ending items need larger or separate evidence (GPT, Claude)?
2. **Sulfur and impurities versus the Phase 1 spec.** What S, P and O levels can melt-route Fe-Ni reach with in-situ slag alone? The proposed limits are Claude's S ≤ 0.05 wt% with ≥98% Fe+Ni+Co, and GPT's ≥95%. This decides the carbonyl cell, and it needs Phase 1 to freeze a material specification before CDR.
3. **Anchoring and reaction loads on rubble piles.** Is a 2 kN pull-out (Claude) achievable, or must tool forces stay at 1–100 N (GPT)? Which anchor family works: microspines, helical screws, penetrators or pads? Scouts (bom-0-1) need to return geotechnical data to answer this.
4. **Containment verification.** Can loss fractions of 10⁻³–10⁻⁴ be measured with a credible upper bound across all particle sizes and velocities? Can the hood clear dust before retraction (Gemini)? What final number will the licensing state accept?
5. **Target availability and grade.** Will scouts confirm a target with accessible native metal, rather than only a metal-rich spectrum, in time for CDR? The candidate envelope is:
   - 5–15 wt% recoverable metal (GPT) or ≥8 wt% (Claude);
   - rotation period ≥ 4–6 h;
   - round-trip Δv ≤ 9 km/s.
6. **Earth-lab need and propulsion maturity.** Is sample return indispensable for product acceptance? Can iodine Hall life and supply close on the pathfinder schedule?

## Recommended Approach

1. **Baseline a mid-scale, single-launch demonstrator built around full-scale critical units.**
   - Take GPT's envelope as the system baseline: ~6–10 t dry, 60–80 kWe BOL, 300 kg–5 t feed, 10–500 kg product.
   - Fly Claude's full 0B-scale versions of the items whose physics do not extrapolate: crucible (≈50 kg batch), cutter head and skirt, canister and docking port, and magnetic-drum width.
   - Reject Gemini's 3 kW / 0.5 kg-per-batch scale. It cannot support a no-waiver TRL 6 claim for 0B.
2. **Use gravity-independent, positively contained processes.**
   - Centrifugal induction melt and cast as the baseline.
   - Forced-feed and mechanically constrained transfers; no ballistic or pneumatic transfer.
   - Nested containment barriers.
   - Carry Claude's carbonyl cell to PDR, deleting it only if ground tests on real chondrite feed reach S ≤ 0.05 wt%.
3. **Set containment per D-03.**
   - Design ceiling ≤1×10⁻³ of mass handled, with no intentional release.
   - Design goal of 10⁻⁴ (GPT's allocation).
   - Mandatory measurement floor ≤10⁻⁴, using carrier or perimeter particle instruments, witness plates and calibrated tracer releases.
   - The licensing state sets the final number from flight data.
4. **Carry costs as ranges with an explicit basis.**
   - **bom-0-12 direct: $1.0–2.5B (point ~$1.6B), 0A only, $0 in 0B.** Basis: ~$100–150k/kg for first-of-kind dry hardware, plus I&T, flight software and reserve.
   - Show a fully burdened attributable view of **$1.8–3.5B** alongside it. This includes launch (bom-0-8, $0.15–0.45B), operations and ground ($0.1–0.35B), shared NRE and contingency, none of it double-counted.
   - Disagreements with round 2: Gemini's ±16% band is too narrow for TRL 2–3 hardware; GPT's $0.6B hardware floor is too low; Claude's $4B tail double-counts external lines.
5. **Propulsion per D-05, with a maturity escape.** Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate. If iodine is not TRL 6 by CDR, fly a qualified noble-gas system on the critical path (Claude's Kr exception) with one iodine string as a life-data source. The owner decides this at SRR.
6. **Retire the lowest-TRL risk early.**
   - Fund a ~300–500 kg LEO free-flyer test of the centrifugal furnace and separator (~$60–150M, in bom-0-11, ~2028–29) before PDR.
   - Impose target-envelope requirements on bom-0-1 now: in-situ geotechnical and native-metal data, rotation ≥ 4–6 h, round-trip Δv ≤ 9 km/s.
7. **Define success and gate timing.**
   - Minimum success comes from the excavation and containment chain alone.
   - KDP-0B may be taken on ~6 months of surface data, with ≥1,000 h of processing and containment calibration complete.
   - Carry a small Earth sample capsule (~$40–100M) as a PDR trade item. Defer bulk SEL1 product return unless bom-0-13 is operating.
   - Keep 0B long-lead procurement gated, so mission loss strands nothing.
